recycling of ferro- and non-ferro metals, cardboard, glass and plastic are recommended to maximize environmental and economic savings simultaneously.

the recycling of ferrous, non-ferrous, cardboard and plastic can be economically and environmentally beneficial for a LEED certified building, and that the recycling of concrete and asphalt is not recommended.
recycling of metals and paper-based materials are the most effective strategies for reducing the carbon footprint and cost of construction debris waste management.

the development and application of a multi-objective decision support framework that integrates environmental and economic impacts to determine the optimal construction waste management strategy for LEED-certification.
the development of a hybrid LCA-based multi-criteria optimization approach to evaluate various construction waste management strategies.

the development of a hybrid LCA and optimization-based decision support tool for the selection of the most environmentally-benign and economically-feasible waste treatment strategy for a LEED certified university building in the United States.

recycling of construction materials is a viable option to minimize the environmental impacts associated with waste treatment.

the results of our study can be used to develop a decision support system to guide the construction waste management of LEED-certified buildings.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the recycling of construction and demolition debris can be economically and environmentally feasible if it is planned and managed in an optimal manner, and the recycling strategies should be based on the characteristics of the materials and the building itself.

recycling of ferromagnetic metals is an environmentally and economically-benign option for LEED-certification, while recycling of non-ferromagnetic metals and asphalt/concrete should be avoided due to high energy consumption during the recycling process.
